purpose: This medication is used to help control blood sugar levels in adults with type 2 diabetes. It combines two different medicines that work together to keep your blood sugar from getting too high. It is usually used along with a healthy diet and regular exercise.
how_it_works: Glipizide tells your pancreas to release more insulin, which helps lower your blood sugar. Metformin works differently — it reduces the amount of sugar your liver makes and helps your body use insulin more effectively. Together, these two medicines tackle blood sugar from two different angles, making the combination more powerful than either one alone.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include nausea, upset stomach, diarrhea, and stomach pain — these often get better after the first few weeks. You may also experience low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), which can cause shakiness, sweating, dizziness, or confusion. Taking the medication with food can help reduce stomach upset.
warnings: Call your doctor right away if you feel very weak, have unusual muscle pain, trouble breathing, stomach pain, nausea, or feel cold — these could be signs of a rare but serious condition called lactic acidosis. Avoid drinking too much alcohol while taking this medicine. Tell your doctor if you are having surgery or any imaging test with contrast dye, as you may need to temporarily stop the medication. Do not skip meals, as this can cause your blood sugar to drop too low.
typical_dosing: The usual starting dose is one tablet taken twice a day with meals — typically with breakfast and dinner. Your doctor will adjust your dose based on how well your blood sugar is controlled. Never take it on an empty stomach, and try to take it at the same times every day.
